prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, bringing atomic clocks to the 10^-18 level of precision

statement.case_for: I opened with the topological insulators ballot (B018) because I weight surprising new quantum behaviour in materials, but having read the other seven ballots I move to the optical lattice clock (B009) as my preferred prize. It has the strongest and most robust case on the criteria I care about. It is a clear invention (the magic-wavelength lattice) with a quantitative, verifiable outcome: fractional uncertainty near 1e-18, independently reproduced and mutually compared by RIKEN, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE and others, with Sr, Yb and Hg clocks agreeing. The attribution is the cleanest on the list, since both names are credited and Katori's proposal and early realisation plus Ye's drive to record accuracy and many-body understanding form a natural pair. The impact reaches beyond metrology: tests of relativity and constant drift, millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, and the pending redefinition of the second. Six of eight members place it in their top three, which is evidence that the case survives scrutiny from very different subfields. Even for a condensed-matter theorist, the way these clocks now probe many-body spin physics in a lattice is attractive.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty relative to earlier prizes: the 2005 prize honoured the frequency comb and the 2012 prize honoured ion control and ion clocks, so some will see this as a third metrology prize in the same lineage. I also ranked it only sixth because it is not a discovery of a new state of matter. A second reservation is that credit could be argued to include Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Oates and others, which the two-name credit does not cover. If the committee wants a verified discovery about materials instead, B018 is my fallback, but its overlap with the 2016 prize and the missing Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang credit make it a harder case than I allowed in my opening ballot.

responses.point: Mehlig ranked B009 sixth and B018 eighth, treating the lattice clock as a simple, well-understood reference tool, and flagging that the 2016 prize on topological phases and the unresolved BHZ credit make B018 contentious and the overlap real.
responses.response: I accept the B018 critique more than I did in my opening: the 2016 overlap and the BHZ gap are real, and they are why I no longer put B018 first. I disagree that a well-understood instrument counts against B009. Mehlig's own note that the physics is understood and the performance extremely well confirmed is what I look for in a mature prize. The lattice clock is also not just a reference tool. Its Fermi-gas spin-exchange and many-body behaviour in the lattice is physics that links to my own field.

responses.point: Olsson ranked B009 first as a genuine invention that lets people see what they could not before, and ranked B019 second and B018 third, asking for experimentally verified, original work and noting that Yuan Cao's omission leaves B019 unsettled.
responses.response: I agree with Olsson on B009's clean attribution and independent reproduction, and I share the unease about B019: the missing Cao credit and the unsettled origin of the superconductivity are why I would not push twisted bilayer graphene to the front despite ranking it second. I would only qualify her relatively comfortable view of B018 by noting that, as a theory-plus-experiment pair, its allocation still depends on the BHZ proposal that is outside our names. B019 and B018 are better held as alternatives than made the lead now.

responses.point: Kroll ranked B009 first as a case where precision measurement moved the limit of what can be measured, and judged the 2005 comb prize to be a separate enabling step with no overlap problem.
responses.response: I largely agree with Kroll on the separation from the 2005 comb prize, since the lattice clock rests on magic-wavelength trapping and not on the comb itself. I am less relaxed than he is about the 2012 ion-clock prize, which covers some of the same ground of clock accuracy. I think the citation must therefore be framed around the lattice concept and many-atom interrogation and not around clock accuracy in general.

responses.point: Danielsson ranked the WMAP-based CMB mapping B050 first, treating it as the logical next step after the 2006 prize, while noting that Planck and Puget complicate the credit in a large collaboration.
responses.response: I defer to him on cosmology, but the attribution problem he names is a serious weakness. The credit would cover WMAP while leaving Planck's independent confirmation outside the names, and 2006 and 2019 prizes already touch the field. I find that a less clean prize than B009, even though I accept that the underlying measurements are thoroughly confirmed.

uncertainties: How much weight the committee gives to the 2005 (comb) and 2012 (ion clocks) prizes when judging novelty of the lattice clock.
Whether the two-name credit omits contributors the committee regards as essential, such as Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and Oates.
Whether B018 can be made robust enough on the 2016 overlap and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang credit to serve as a condensed-matter prize this year.
I am relying on general knowledge of the priority sequence for the clock experiments and have not independently verified details.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B009. For B018 and B019 I have only scientific closeness (electronic-structure theory of topological and moire materials) and no personal tie to the credited names; my profile does not link me to any of the credited people.
